# Percutaneous Left Atrial Appendage Closure: A Narrative Review

## Introduction

Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common sustained arrhythmia and a major cause of ischemic stroke. The left atrial appendage (LAA) is the dominant source of cardioembolism in nonvalvular AF: in early surgical and autopsy series, the overwhelming majority of left atrial thrombi were localized to the appendage, providing the anatomical rationale for mechanical LAA exclusion. Left atrial appendage obliteration was historically a routine part of modern "curative" operations for nonrheumatic atrial fibrillation such as the maze and corridor procedures, and reviews of prior reports evaluated the presence and location of left atrial thrombus by transesophageal echocardiography, autopsy, or operation.[1] Although oral anticoagulation (OAC) is highly effective, it carries a substantial bleeding burden and is frequently underused or contraindicated, motivating the development of percutaneous LAA closure (LAAC).

## Foundational randomized evidence

The pivotal PROTECT AF trial established proof of concept. This multicenter study randomized 707 patients with nonvalvular AF and at least one risk factor to the Watchman device or continued warfarin in a 2:1 ratio to determine whether LAAC was noninferior to warfarin for stroke prevention.[2] After 2.3±1.1 years of follow-up, the composite primary efficacy endpoint rates were 3.0% and 4.3% per 100 patient-years in the Watchman and warfarin groups, respectively, meeting criteria for noninferiority.[3] Longer follow-up confirmed and extended these findings into a randomized clinical trial publication.[4]

Because PROTECT AF identified a periprocedural safety hazard, the confirmatory PREVAIL trial was undertaken. This multicenter randomized trial assessed LAAC with the Watchman versus warfarin in patients with a CHADS2 score ≥2, enrolling 407 patients (269 device, 138 control).[5] At 18 months the first coprimary efficacy endpoint did not achieve prespecified noninferiority, the second coprimary endpoint (late stroke or systemic embolism) did achieve noninferiority, and early safety events fell to 2.2%, significantly lower than in PROTECT AF.[6] A patient-level meta-analysis of these trials supported equivalence to warfarin with reduced bleeding and mortality.[7] The PROTECT AF trial demonstrated that LAAC was equivalent to warfarin for preventing stroke but had a high rate of complications, and 5-year pooled outcomes reaffirmed durable efficacy with significantly less hemorrhagic and disabling stroke and lower cardiovascular mortality.[8]

## Patients ineligible for anticoagulation and registry experience

The ASAP study addressed patients who could not take warfarin. It assessed LAA closure in nonvalvular AF patients ineligible for warfarin therapy, since PROTECT AF had only included warfarin candidates, supporting feasibility without an initial warfarin bridge.[9] Real-world data corroborated trial findings: the EWOLUTION registry reported high implant success and favorable peri-procedural safety with the Watchman device.[10] The NCDR LAAO Registry described in-hospital adverse event rates for Watchman procedures in the United States during its first three years, with major in-hospital adverse events in 2.16% of patients, most commonly pericardial effusion requiring intervention (1.39%) and major bleeding (1.25%), while stroke (0.17%) and death (0.19%) were rare—lower than in the pivotal trials despite higher-risk patients.[11]

## Comparison with direct oral anticoagulants

The PRAGUE-17 trial provided the first head-to-head comparison against DOACs. This multicenter randomized noninferiority trial compared LAAC with DOACs in high-risk patients with a history of bleeding, prior cardioembolism on OAC, and/or elevated CHA2DS2-VASc and HAS-BLED scores.[12] In long-term follow-up, LAAC remained noninferior to DOACs for preventing major cardiovascular, neurological, or bleeding events, and nonprocedural bleeding was significantly reduced with LAAC.[13]

## Device evolution

Newer devices have improved sealing and safety. The Amulet IDE trial evaluated the dual-seal Amulet occluder against the Watchman, and the Amulet was noninferior for safety and effectiveness and superior for LAA occlusion, though procedure-related complications were higher with the Amulet and decreased with operator experience.[14] Five-year outcomes confirmed durable performance of both devices.[15] The next-generation Watchman FLX was assessed in PINNACLE FLX, a single-arm IDE trial at 29 US sites enrolling 400 patients, which established procedural safety and closure efficacy against performance goals for the legacy device,[16] with favorable two-year results [17] and reassuring contemporary registry outcomes.[18]

## Complications: device-related thrombus and peri-device leak

Two device-specific concerns dominate surveillance. Device-related thrombus (DRT) after LAAO is uncommon (~3.8%) but is associated with a 4- to 5-fold increase in ischemic events.[19] In a large French cohort, the incidence, predictors, and prognosis of device thrombus were examined,[20] and pooled trial data quantified DRT incidence and its predictors.[21] Multicenter registries have further characterized thrombus features and management,[22] including Amulet-specific data,[23] and demonstrated that about one-third of DRT events follow an unfavorable course associated with higher thromboembolic risk.[24] Peri-device leak (PDL) is similarly important: on adjusted analysis, peri-device leak on the 1-year transesophageal study was associated with a higher rate of thromboembolism,[25] a finding echoed in the NCDR registry,[26] with delayed leaks evolving over time.[27] An early PROTECT AF substudy first examined the clinical impact of incomplete closure.[28]

## Antithrombotic strategy and net clinical benefit

Optimal post-implant antithrombotic therapy remains debated; propensity-matched analyses have compared anticoagulation versus antiplatelet regimens after closure.[29] Importantly, pooled randomized data established a favorable net clinical benefit of LAAC over warfarin.[30]

## Future directions

The recent OPTION trial extended LAAC into the post-ablation population. Among adults with nonvalvular AF and elevated CHA2DS2-VASc scores, AF ablation followed by LAA occlusion was noninferior for embolic events and superior for bleeding compared with ablation followed by anticoagulation.[31—reference uses index 31 below]. Contemporary guidelines now incorporate LAAC as a reasonable option for selected patients with elevated stroke risk and contraindications to long-term anticoagulation.[31]
